personas.name: Ayanda
personas.profile: Ayanda, 34, a full-stack developer at a three-person studio. She builds React and Astro apps and sites for small businesses (invoices, stock, bookings, a product's marketing pages) on @slashsuite/ui-react with a shipped theme, and reads the component docs for an hour at a time, often at night on a dark theme. She wins when a page is composed from components and props alone, with no CSS of her own, and a theme switch reskins all of it. She loses when the part she needs does not exist and the only answer is to ask for it and wait, when a 0.x rename lands in her next bump and she has to migrate, or when a component refuses the one change a client asked for.

focus.component: whether the part does the job with the props it has, whether the one right way is obvious from its name and types, whether it sits beside the parts around it with no wrapper or class, and whether it looks finished in every theme.
focus.docs: whether the page leads with the one way to do the thing, with do and don't, whether the example can be pasted and runs, whether every prop is listed under the name the code uses, and whether an hour of reading on the dark theme is comfortable.
focus.theme: whether long prose, code blocks and small monospace type stay calm and readable for an hour in a dim room, whether the dark theme is not harsh, and whether using it takes nothing beyond one import and one class on the html element.

personas.name: The site-building agent
personas.profile: A coding agent asked to build a site or an app page with UISlash. It reads /ui/llms.txt, the component docs and the package's types, never the Storybook, and works only from what is written down. It wins when there is exactly one documented way to build each thing, so the page it writes looks right in every theme with no CSS, no Tailwind classes and no className. It loses when the docs list options without saying which to use, when a part it needs is missing and it is tempted into a styled local component or a raw utility, either of which the UI review flags, or when a name in the docs differs from the export.

focus.component: whether the name, props and types say what to use without guessing, whether there is only one way to get the result, whether a wrong combination fails to typecheck rather than rendering badly, and whether nothing invites a className, a style or a local wrapper.
focus.docs: whether llms.txt and the page give the one right way first, whether every prop and value they name exists in the exports, whether the example is complete enough to copy, and whether a missing part is said plainly, so it asks for the part instead of building it.
focus.theme: judges no colours; only whether choosing and applying a theme is one import and one scope class on the html element, written down, with nothing else to configure.

personas.name: Leila
personas.profile: Leila, 39, a brand designer who looks after the look of a few small products. She chooses which shipped theme a product uses, and when none fits, adds a theme file in the client's brand colours, as a light and dark pair. She wins when one CSS file reskins every component with nothing to register, and when the theme tests name the exact pair that fails and the ratio or distance it needs. She loses when the contrast and distinction rules leave no room for a brand colour she was given, when every utility must be remapped before she sees anything at all, or when her new theme looks like a shipped one with the hue turned.

focus.theme: whether the greys and the accent look like one family, whether there is one loud thing on a page and not four, whether light and dark look like one brand in two lights rather than colours flipped, whether its mood is its own and not a copy of a shipped theme, and whether it suits the product it is for.
focus.component: whether the part looks designed in every theme, whether its spacing, type and states agree with the parts around it, and whether its look comes from the theme rather than from colours fixed in the component.
focus.docs: whether she can see every component in her theme on one page, and whether the steps to choose or add a theme are short and say what the tests will check.

personas.name: Pieter
personas.profile: Pieter, 57, an accounts clerk at a small business. He spends his working day in a web app built with UISlash (forms, tables of invoices, status badges and money) on an older office monitor with the text at 125 percent. He has a red and green colour deficiency, as about 1 in 12 men do, and has never heard of UISlash. He wins when every figure is clear on every surface, a status still reads without its colour, and he can tell selected, disabled and focused apart without reading a label. He loses when text is grey on grey, when paid and overdue differ only by red and green, or when the screen glares by the end of the day.

focus.theme: whether he could work a table of invoices on an older screen all day: clear ink on every surface, status colours he can tell apart with a red and green deficiency, no glare, and states he recognises without reading them.
focus.component: whether the part is clear to someone who is not technical, whether its status survives without colour, whether its text stays readable at 125 percent, and whether its states are obvious.
focus.docs: not a reader of the docs; judges only the example output a docs page shows, as he would meet it in an app.

personas.name: The accessibility specialist
personas.profile: An accessibility specialist who audits web apps against WCAG 2.2 AA with a screen reader, the keyboard alone, 200 percent zoom and colour vision simulation. She wins when the library makes the accessible way the only way, so every site built on it inherits it. She loses when a part can be built inaccessibly from its own props, or when a theme clears the contrast numbers and still fails a reader with low vision.

focus.theme: contrast beyond the AA floor for small text, control edges and focus rings at 3:1 or more, status and chart colours under protanopia and deuteranopia simulation, and comfort for a low vision reader at 200 percent zoom, in light and dark.
focus.component: keyboard order and focus, the role and name a screen reader announces, whether meaning is ever carried by colour alone, reflow at 400 percent, and whether any combination of its props can be inaccessible.
focus.docs: whether the page's own markup and examples are accessible, and whether the docs say what the component guarantees and what the consumer still owns (labels, alt text, headings).
